toc.title: When the foundation isn't there yet

blocks.p: How do you self-regulate through extreme situations, and is that even possible? It's a common question, and it can look a few different ways. You might relate to it. I want to bring some clarity to it and help you identify some next steps for your own self-regulation in extreme situations.

One member asked it this way: how does someone who doesn't have self-regulation, and doesn't have co-regulation, get through situations like medical appointments, where it's fast and disconnected and potentially triggering? How would someone combat that?
That's basically a worst-case scenario: what do I do now?

It reminds me of parents who show up to a parenting group. They don't have the parenting skills, they don't have patience, and they've got their own stuff they have to deal with, traumas and whatnot. And they say, "My kid's hitting me, they swear at me, and they won't go to school. What do I do?"
You've hit the bottom. We're way down here, and now you want to dig your way out. Of course you want the answer to that. But I don't know if there is a simple answer.
We tend to wait until things are at their worst before we ask, "Well, what do I do next?" That's where anticipating these events comes in.
We could throw out ideas for days, and they could be helpful. Here are some.

Bring a co-regulator. Maybe there's someone close to you who can go with you and be an advocate: speak up for you, or ask questions along with you, because they know you're going to be in a really triggered state. Someone who can just check in with you and give you a hug afterwards. That's an avenue, if you have it.

Bring something that anchors you in safety. What if you don't have that person? You could bring something with you that anchors you in safety. But that means you have to practice it ahead of time. If you know you're going to your doctor's appointment and you're going to have an aggressive, fight kind of energy within you, maybe you bring something you can squeeze, to release a bit of that energy before the doctor comes in. Or keep it in your pocket and squeeze it while you talk to them. A fidget, a sensory thing that just lowers the amount of defensive state.

Release it afterwards. Maybe you don't have access to anything yet. You don't know what anchors you quite yet. So afterwards, maybe you do something that helps alleviate it. Scream into a pillow. Scream in your car. Rip something up. Release the energy in some way that's not ideal, but good enough to recover.

Prepare what you need from the visit. If you know you're going to get thrown way off track and lose your questions, bring them written down for the doctor: this is what I want out of this meeting, and I need this answered. And you can know ahead of time that it's going to be difficult and they might be dismissive, but that it's also okay for you to be a little upset and say, "No, I have to have an answer for this. This has to make sense to me," or, "I have to have this referral," or whatever it is.
I don't know if there's ever going to be a doctor's visit that goes perfectly, or that is not triggering. But maybe it'll be less so next time.

A lot of this comes down to preparation. If you have no self-regulation, or almost none, and no co-regulator, the question becomes: how do we soften the blow of what we're about to go through? That requires us to prepare ahead of time.

And ultimately, it comes down to eventually building the capacity to self-regulate: building the strength of the vagal brake through more and more anchoring in safety. That has to be done outside the context of those visits.

We don't want to wait to be thrown into the fire. If you just started playing baseball, and you don't know how to swing a bat and hit a ball, and all of a sudden you're out in front of thousands of people in a Major League game, you're not ready for it. It's not going to go well. It'll probably be a disaster.
So can you practice, in some capacity, ahead of time? Here's how I'd prioritize it.

ol: Recognize your states. First off, can you recognize these different states? That's the basic knowledge of the Polyvagal Theory.

Anchor in safety, away from the trigger. Then can you apply that knowledge to your safety state in particular, and develop the capacity to anchor in safety more and more? This happens out of the context of even thinking about the things you know are triggering. It's just what helps you feel better: a sense of goodness, or lighter, or more connected to yourself.
Anchor around the context. Then, eventually, can you do more specific, planned anchoring around the context? Before you even leave for the doctor's appointment, can you do things that are anchoring?

blocks.p: For the second step, ask: what helps me feel good? What do I like? And can I spend more time doing that, but a bit more mindfully? If you like cooking, cool. Can you spend more time really experiencing what it's like to cook? Can you really smell? Can you look at the colors and really take them in? Can you really feel what you're doing, maybe a bit more slowly? That's anchoring in safety, and the mindfulness of it helps build those pathways. It builds familiarity with what it feels like to be safe, so you have more of a reference point.

For the third step, here's an example from my own life. I'm terrified of heights. If I'm in a car up high, it can send me into a panic attack. Yes, I want to anchor and ground myself during the panic attack. But can I also do it directly before a certain bridge that I'm more triggered by? Can I do something twenty minutes before that? How far back can I go in the context, while still being around it, and anchor in my car, on the way to the thing?

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: One member pointed out that this may be why anxious people research as much as they do. In the medical setting, all of a sudden they become experts in how everything works. It may or may not help in the moment, but it can keep building that tolerance.
It's a long process. Potentially a very long process.

If you have more of a shock trauma, say you got in a car accident and now you're afraid of getting in cars, it could happen that you do some polar bear trauma releasing, you shake and tremble, it comes out of your system, and you're no longer in that frozen state around cars. The next time you get in a car, it won't be nearly as triggering. "Oh, wow, I really let it out." That could happen, I suppose.

But other things are more long-term, and not necessarily a shock you went through. With me and heights, I can't identify any specific thing that led me to be terrified of them. It's always kind of been there. Being up high is more anxiety-inducing than pleasurable for me, to say the least.

So I'm more mindful of it, and I challenge myself here and there to feel some of that defensive energy. I'll look over the balcony of a two-story building, just to feel it, and I notice it's becoming more tolerable. When I drive, bridges are less triggering. I'm not going to go bungee jumping, scare the heck out of myself, and try to release whatever might be inside of me. I don't know if that would help. Instead, I'm going gradually. And I notice: this used to be really unsettling for me, and now I didn't even notice it. Maybe I'm even able to be more playful about it. You notice the absence.

It's a long process that requires deliberate anchoring, mindfulness, and practice. My example is pretty light compared to what a lot of people go through, but the basic idea is the same. With something like C-PTSD or sexual trauma, it would probably be a much longer process, and more challenging and more difficult, of course.

blocks.h: When the foundation isn't there yet

blocks.p: I was once on a radio show where they had callers, and a woman said, "I have sexual trauma, but I want to be more intimate with my partner. How do I do that?" It's the same kind of question as the parent asking, "My kids are throwing things at me and swearing and running out of the house. What do I do?"

You haven't done the steps required yet. You haven't laid the foundation. There's no groundwork. We could throw a ton of ideas at you, but in that moment, it's going to be a lot more difficult to just plug these things in.
Deb Dana put it this way when she was on the podcast:

q: When you dysregulate, your prefrontal cortex does not go along for the ride with you.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana: Book 2 and COVID-19 (episode 54)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/98a53db3-770b-483d-ad74-40256d4c6b3a)

blocks.p: I think a lot of therapy runs into this, especially the more cognitive and behavior-focused kinds: "When you notice that you feel this way, just do this instead." Or, "If you notice these thoughts in your head, replace them with some other thoughts." It's a great idea. It makes sense. But in those moments, it doesn't seem to go anywhere. You can't flip it off like a switch.
